accuracy.reason: Cards 1-8 correctly scope persistence, requirements, record/specialized models, overlapping capabilities, index/copy/distribution costs and CAP. Live primary documentation supports critical claims; product labels are not treated as guarantees.

evidence.quote: CAP is a trade-off during network failures. A database type, such as relational or document, does not determine its CAP guarantees.

mechanisms.reason: Cards 1-3 connect layout to query/update work; card 4 explains partition grouping, graph edges and numerical similarity; cards 5-6 explain capabilities and maintenance costs; card 7 traces the isolated-reader impossibility; card 8 connects measurement to choice.

evidence.quote: Explain both the benefit and the cost. Check the actual product, deployment, and operation before claiming a guarantee.

coherence.reason: All eight objectives build in prerequisite order. Source-inspected diagrams compare the same product as table/document/key layouts, illustrate query-specific group/path/similarity, and pair benefits/costs without inventing guarantees. Shared renderer/CSS inspected, not executed.

evidence.quote: A flexible document still needs rules. A table can hold flexible fields. Compare the data layout and supported guarantees, not just the label.

decisions.reason: Requirements and measured queries lead the choice, including recovery capability, index write cost, duplicated-data coordination and extra-store operations. CAP is bounded to affected operations during communication failures.

evidence.quote: Requirements lead to a model, queries, and guarantees. Product names come after that reasoning.

clarity.reason: Terms are defined and examples aid comparison. The range of models and capabilities is broad for eight cards, but no prerequisite needed for the stated foundational objectives is missing.

evidence.quote: Partition lookups, relationship paths, and similarity searches are different workloads. Name the query before choosing a specialized store.

outcomes.reason: All six criteria satisfied: database persistence and operations, layout effects, recovery limits, records/relationships/query/update patterns, correctness/growth/latency/operations and category limits.

All six criteria satisfied: rows/columns/joins, embedded document read/update tradeoff, known-key limits, query-led partition grouping versus network partitions, graph nodes/edges/traversal and numeric-vector similarity without equality or truth guarantees.

All six criteria satisfied: spatial/vector overlap, actual feature/performance/guarantee assessment, separate-store synchronization and operations, index space/write costs, duplicate-update coordination and distributed partial-failure costs.

All six criteria satisfied: replication and communication split, one-copy consistency versus every-node response availability, affected-operation/configuration scope, requirement-led selection, accepted costs/recovery and measurement-based reconsideration without mandatory vendors or multiple stores.

sourceChecks.claim: Live PostgreSQL Concepts defines relational stored data; its backup documentation confirms recoverability depends on complete coordinated backups. The application/layout coupling is consistent with the demonstrated query models.

Live PostgreSQL JSON types confirms relational JSON support. MongoDB transaction documentation confirms document transactions with configured guarantees. These substantiate requirements-led comparison rather than exclusive category assumptions.

Live MongoDB data modeling describes embedded records/references and access-pattern-driven layout; PostgreSQL Concepts and transaction examples support relational records/queries. Diagram product layouts preserve the same data and show changed retrieval work.

Live Cassandra logical modeling ties partition keys and table organization to required queries and data size/read performance. Neo4j primary concepts supports nodes/relationships/traversal; pgvector README supports numeric distance and approximate recall/speed tradeoffs. None establishes factual correctness from similarity.

Live PostGIS documentation plus its official introduction describes spatial types, indexes and spatial functions integrated with relational data. Live pgvector README confirms PostgreSQL vector search and measurable speed/recall costs; feature overlap does not imply equal workloads.

Live PostgreSQL indexes introduction explains suitable-query lookup benefits and synchronization overhead. MongoDB modeling and Cassandra layouts support duplicate read/update tradeoffs; distributed copies incur communication and recovery work rather than eliminating it.

Live FoundationDB CAP page defines current-copy reads and every-node operation availability; its two-node split explains unseen writes and distinguishes client-visible uptime from CAP availability. Lesson correctly avoids the universal choose-any-two slogan.

Live PostgreSQL Concepts supplies representation/query foundations; the inspected MongoDB, Cassandra and index sources substantiate workload-led choices and maintenance costs. Final card offers a bounded reasoning method rather than claiming a universal product winner.
